newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Jump seen in Feb U.S. housing starts.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Jump seen in Feb U.S. housing starts.

text.p: Sound fundamentals coupled with kind weather in the Northeast and upper Midwest probably pushed U.S. housing starts higher in February, experts said.

An eventual jump in housing starts should offer nourishment to the economy this quarter following two quarters of being a drag, said Stuart Hoffman, senior economist at PNC Financial Corp. "It means that, in addition to strong consumer spending helping the economy this quarter, you should also get a little bit of a kick from housing," said Hoffman.
Based on preliminary results from a Reuters poll, the consensus appeared to be calling for an annual rate of about 1.43 million starts in February, up from 1.35 million in January.
The report is slated for release by the Department of Commerce at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Tuesday.

Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc, who forecast 1.485 million starts in February, said most of the surge will be weather related, but it will not be a purely weather phenomenon. "I think you have good underlying fundamentals as well," he said.
Moran cited strong labor markets and relatively low interest rates as the lure for prospective home buyers, naturally leading to a pickup in building activity.

For instance, the rise in February payrolls, where construction jobs grew by 109,000, was followed by a sharp increase in February sales at building materials stores. And analysts said that should translate into a pickup in single-family housing.

"I see it as very strong fundamentals in terms of confidence, income growth, and the fact that building permits have surpassed housing starts for two months, which is very abnormal," said Don Maude, chief U.S. economist at Scotia Capital Markets Inc.
Maude explained that starts are usually above permits. He said the current reverse in trend showed pipeline demand from the permits, which should further strengthen starts.

Despite the fact that economic fundamentals look relatively favorable, some analysts caution the rebound in starts will be short-lived. A rise in mortgage rates now will hurt housing starts in the second and third quarters, they said.
"I wouldn't view (February) as a renewed resurgence in housing market activity. I think basically, housing will flatten out over the next couple of months, " added Maude.
